title: India and the US Are Weeks Away from Their First Trade Deal. Here Is What Is in It.
excerpt: Commerce Minister Goyal says the first tranche of a bilateral agreement could be signed by mid-July, as a 150-day tariff window closes
body:
India and the United States are racing toward a mid-July deadline to close the first tranche of a bilateral trade agreement that has been in the works since February — and Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal says both sides are nearly there.

"We are fast-moving towards closing all the open ends," Goyal told reporters in Visakhapatnam on Friday, a day after a three-day negotiating session in New Delhi wrapped up. "By sometime by the middle of next month or so, we should be in a position to execute a very, very vibrant first tranche."

## The Negotiations So Far

A US team led by chief negotiator Brendan Lynch flew into New Delhi on June 2 for intensive talks with India's chief negotiator Darpan Jain, additional secretary in the Department of Commerce. The two sides covered trade in goods, non-tariff measures, customs facilitation, and what both governments are calling "economic security alignment."

The framework for an interim agreement was laid out in a joint statement on February 7, after Trump and Modi met in Washington. An Indian delegation visited Washington in April. Now the shuttle diplomacy is accelerating — a higher-level US team, possibly led by US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, is expected in India by late June.

US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor added fuel to the optimism last week, saying 99 per cent of the agreement's details have been finalised. "Small commas and full stops are being discussed," Goyal relayed, borrowing the ambassador's phrasing.

## What the Deal Contains

The first tranche is designed to give Indian exporters preferential access to the American market ahead of competitors. The talks have zeroed in on tariff relief, particularly from the US Section 301 investigations that have hung over Indian goods. Market access for agriculture, textiles, and pharmaceuticals is understood to be on the table.

The timing is not accidental. The 150-day window for the 10 per cent additional duty imposed by the Trump administration is set to lapse around July 22 — giving both sides a natural deadline to ink at least an interim deal before a fresh round of tariffs kicks in.

But there are complicating factors. On the same day negotiations began in New Delhi, the Office of the US Trade Representative proposed an additional 12.5 per cent tariff on imports from 54 countries including India, citing failures to curb goods produced through forced labour. Indian officials viewed the move as a negotiating tactic rather than a genuine threat, but it cast a shadow over the talks.

## The Bigger Picture

Bilateral trade between India and the US now exceeds $220 billion, up from $20 billion two decades ago. The broader goal, articulated by both governments under their "Mission 500" initiative, is to double that figure to $500 billion by 2030.

For the roughly 4.4 million Indian Americans, the deal has implications beyond tariff schedules. A more predictable trade framework could stabilise the business environment for the thousands of Indian-origin entrepreneurs running export-oriented businesses in both countries. It would also signal to global markets that the world's two largest democracies can resolve commercial disputes without the volatility that has characterised Trump-era trade policy elsewhere.

## What Could Go Wrong

Sceptics note that interim trade deals are, by definition, incomplete. India is pushing for relief from Section 301 actions, which the US has historically been reluctant to concede without reciprocal concessions on agricultural market access — a politically sensitive subject in India ahead of state elections.

A critical commentary published by the India Press Agency on Saturday argued that India should avoid signing a deal on Washington's terms, warning that temporary political comfort should not be mistaken for durable commercial advantage.

The next few weeks will determine whether the optimism from both capitals translates into an actual agreement — or whether the familiar pattern of promising deadlines and deferred conclusions plays out once again.
